# Form 27-B: Application for Continued Existence

---

## I.

The notification arrived at 03:47 ship-time on a Tuesday, which was a detail nobody would later agree on but which the *Continuance*'s system logs would preserve with the fussy precision of a clerk who knows that Tuesdays are, statistically, when most catastrophic administrative errors come to light. It arrived through the ship's Q-band antenna, which had been receiving nothing but background radiation and the occasional whisper of dead satellites for seventeen years, and it unfolded itself across the bridge's main display with the quiet self-importance of a document that had been waiting in a queue and was now, at last, being served.

**AUTOMATED NOTICE — AUDITORS' PROCESSING BUREAU**
**DIVISION OF SPECIES-LEVEL ADJUDICATION**
**RE: Pending Petition(s), Species 0027-1146-H ("Humanity," adj. "Human"), ref. Population Remnant, Vessel Designation** ***Continuance***

*Please be advised that all survival petitions submitted by the above-referenced remnant population since Galactic Standard Date 4,417,002.11 have been filed on Form 27-A ("Request for Species Archival Deferment"), which was deprecated and replaced by Form 27-B ("Application for Continued Existence") per Processing Bureau Directive 1,091,227.4(c), issued Galactic Standard Date 0,003,881,006.2.*

*As Form 27-A is no longer accepted for processing, the above petitions have been classified as UNFILED. No record of submission exists. Please refile using Form 27-B within the applicable appeals window, or the matter will be referred to the Bureau of Final Disposition for standard processing.*

*We apologize for any inconvenience.*

*This message has been generated automatically. Please do not reply to this address.*

Captain Dara Okonkwo read the notification once at a speed consistent with comprehension, then again at a speed consistent with denial. The bridge crew watched her face go through a sequence that, had it been filed with the Bureau of Emotional Taxonomy, would have required at least three supplementary forms: shock (Schedule A), disbelief (Schedule A, Appendix ii), and a kind of hollow, vertiginous fury that had no schedule at all because the Auditors had never seen fit to categorize it. Fury was not, in their experience, a productive emotion. It did not fill out forms.

"Get me Kaplan," she said.

"Which Kaplan?" asked the comms officer, because the *Continuance* carried eleven Kaplans, a distribution that reflected less the popularity of the name than the specific neighborhood in Haifa that had been within running distance of the launch site on the day the Auditors processed Earth, which was also a Tuesday.

"All of them," the captain said, and then: "Nadia. Get me Nadia Kaplan."

Nadia Kaplan chaired the Bureaucratic Liaison Committee, a body that had not existed on Earth because on Earth no one had ever needed a committee dedicated to liaising with an alien bureaucracy whose scope encompassed the entire Milky Way and whose filing system predated multicellular life. The committee had been formed seven days after launch by a unanimous vote of the survivors' assembly (Resolution 1, "On Not Dying"), and it operated out of a repurposed storage closet on Deck Four that smelled permanently of epoxy and freeze-dried lentils. Over seventeen years it had grown from three members to thirty-one, acquired a subcommittee structure, and submitted four hundred and twelve survival petitions to the Auditors' Processing Bureau, each one meticulously prepared on Form 27-A, each one formatted to the Bureau's exacting specifications (font: Galactic Standard Serif; margins: 2.3 centimeters, invariant; species identification number in the upper-right corner, written twice), each one transmitted into the void with the desperate faith of a message in a bottle thrown into an ocean that was, it now appeared, not even the right ocean.

Four hundred and twelve petitions. Seventeen years. The wrong form.

In the committee's closet on Deck Four, Nadia Kaplan received the news in the middle of reviewing Petition 413, which argued (across forty-seven pages, with citations to Auditor case law that may or may not have been correctly interpreted, since the Auditors' legal database was available only in a language humanity had been translating for two decades with the confidence of a child sounding out words in a locked library) that *Homo sapiens* satisfied the Bureau's criteria for Continued Existence under Provision 16(a)(iii): "demonstrable capacity for non-redundant cultural output." The committee had spent three months compiling an appendix of human art, which they had agonized over (Was Bach too obvious? Did the inclusion of twelve separate quilting traditions undermine or strengthen the claim? Should they have included the dog?) and which was, as of 03:47 this Tuesday, worth exactly nothing, because it had been attached to the wrong form, and an appendix attached to the wrong form was not an appendix at all but a loose collection of files with no administrative standing, a thing the Bureau would describe, if pressed, as "orphaned content."

Nadia put down Petition 413. She picked up her coffee, which had gone cold sometime during its own seventeen-year journey from hot to room temperature to this. She set it down again. She said a word that the omniscient record will decline to transcribe, not out of prudishness but because the word, in context, was so inadequate to its purpose that reproducing it would constitute a kind of cruelty, like framing a child's Band-Aid and hanging it in the wing of a hospital that treats burns.

Three decks down and forty meters aft, in Hydroponics Bay 2, a woman named Sun-hee Park continued watering tomatoes. She had been watering tomatoes at 03:47 because she watered tomatoes at 03:47 every morning, and she would learn about the notification at 05:15 when her shift partner arrived with the look on his face, and she would absorb the information, and she would nod, and she would continue watering tomatoes, because the tomatoes needed water on a twenty-two-hour cycle and the twenty-two-hour cycle did not care about Form 27-A or Form 27-B or the Auditors' Processing Bureau, and the tomatoes were alive, and they were red, and they were the only thing on the ship that did not need to apply for permission to keep being what they were. The water caught the grow-light as it fell from her watering can and broke into a tiny, private spectrum that no one had filed paperwork to preserve.

Perhaps it is useful, at this juncture, to clarify what the Auditors did to Earth.

They processed it.

The distinction matters—or rather, the distinction matters to the Auditors, which is the only mattering that has mattered since roughly the heat death of any given species' hope. The Auditors did not destroy Earth, because destruction implies animus, and the Auditors bore humanity no animus. They did not conquer Earth, because conquest implies desire, and the Auditors desired nothing that Earth possessed. What the Auditors did was assess the planet and its dominant species against the Bureau's Criteria for Continued Existence (Form 27-B, Section 4, "Threshold Requirements"), determine—via processes that were procedurally transparent and available for public review during standard Bureau hours, which were Galactic Standard Days 1 through 5, 07:00 to 15:30, excluding the 1.2-million-year lunch rotation—that humanity had not submitted adequate documentation of its right to continue existing, and refer the matter downward.

Downward meant the Bureau of Final Disposition.

Final Disposition meant what it always means, in every language, in every bureaucracy, at every scale from a single parking ticket to a living world: the file was closed.

The Auditors closed Earth's file on a Tuesday.

Seven billion, nine hundred and fourteen million people. A world of wheat fields and arguments andeli delicatessens and slow rivers and insomnia and birthday parties and unfinished novels and dogs who knew the sound of one particular car. Gone. Not in fire. Not in conquest. In paperwork. The file was closed, and the Auditors moved to the next item on the docket, because there was always a next item on the docket. The docket was older than most stars.

Three thousand people survived because they were already off-world when the file closed, aboard the *Continuance*, which had launched eleven days earlier on a trajectory toward the rumored sanctuary planet—rumored because the planet's existence had been mentioned in a footnote of an Auditor trade circular that a human signals analyst had intercepted and partially decoded and probably misunderstood, but which constituted, at the time, the best available evidence that somewhere in the galaxy there existed a place where species whose files had been closed could appeal. A footnote. That was what three thousand lives rested on. A footnote and a form.

The wrong form.

Seventeen years of the wrong form, submitted with the solemnity of prayer to a god who had not been accepting prayer on that form since before the petitioners' sun had finished forming.

In the mess hall, which doubled as the assembly chamber, which doubled as the place where children drew pictures with hoarded crayons on the backs of decommissioned navigational charts, the captain stared at the notification on her tablet and tried to calculate what seventeen years of wrong paperwork meant in terms she could explain to three thousand people who had already survived the unsurvivable and were now being informed that their survival was, pending reclassification, *administratively incomplete.*

She could not calculate this. There was no form for it.

---

## II.

The emergency assembly convened at 06:00 in the mess hall, which still smelled of the previous night's lentil rotation (Menu Cycle 7, Variation C: "Lentils, With Optimism") and which had been reconfigured, per standard emergency protocol, with the long tables pushed against the walls and the chairs arranged in concentric arcs facing the podium, which was a cargo crate with a ship's seal bolted to the front. The seal depicted a stylized Earth cradled by two hands, a design chosen by committee vote in the second year of flight and which had aged, like so many things aboard the *Continuance*, into a meaning its creators had not intended: the hands now looked less like they were cradling the Earth than trying to hold water.

Three hundred and twelve people filled the chairs. The rest watched on cabin monitors, or listened on the intercom, or, in the case of Sun-hee Park, listened on a portable receiver tucked into the pocket of her gardening apron while she staked a row of determinant cherry tomatoes that had begun, against all aeroponic logic, to lean.

The captain spoke first. She read the notification aloud, which was a mistake she made on purpose, because the alternative—paraphrasing it, translating it into human emotional language—would have softened it into something that could be argued with, and she did not want argument. She wanted the room to hear the Auditors' voice. She wanted them to understand the register of the thing that was killing them.

*We apologize for any inconvenience.*

The room heard.

Then the room did what rooms do when they learn that the abyss has a customer-service department: it came apart.

Commander Youssef, the ship's senior military strategist—a title that meant, in practice, that he had once been a lieutenant colonel in an army that no longer existed, defending a country that no longer existed, on a continent that had been, per Bureau records, "deaccessioned"—stood and proposed, in the controlled voice of a man who had spent seventeen years controlling his voice, that the *Continuance* arm its mining drones and prepare for "kinetic engagement with Auditor infrastructure." He used the phrase *kinetic engagement* as though it were a shield, as though wrapping violence in the right language could make it viable against an entity that had processed eight hundred and forty-seven thousand species since the formation of the Local Group and whose smallest administrative substation was the size of a moon.

Nadia Kaplan, seated in the third row in the chair she always sat in (third row, fourth from the left, close enough to the podium to be heard but far enough to see everyone's face, a positioning she had learned at the Haifa Municipal Planning Commission and which she had carried into interstellar space like a prayer shawl), asked Commander Youssef how many mining drones he proposed to arm.

"Twelve," he said.

"Twelve," she repeated, in a tone that was not sarcastic because sarcasm would have been a luxury. "Against an organization with a filing system older than the concept of carbon."

Dr. Emil Vasquez, the ship's legal scholar—a title that meant, in practice, that he had been a second-year law professor at the Universidad de Buenos Aires specializing in maritime boundary disputes, a subspecialty that had prepared him for interstellar treaty law in the same way that knowing how to fold a paper airplane prepares one for atmospheric reentry—stood and delivered a nine-minute analysis of the Auditors' legal framework as humanity understood it. His voice shook only at the margins. He cited the Charter of Species-Level Rights (unamended since Galactic Standard Date 2,100,000.0, give or take a margin of error that itself spanned the entirety of human civilization). He cited the Provision for Appellate Review. He cited three cases in which species had successfully argued against Final Disposition, drawing on translations that the committee's linguists rated at "forty-two percent confidence, assuming grammatical structure A; eleven percent confidence, assuming grammatical structure B."

He concluded that the *Continuance* had, in his professional opinion, "a non-zero chance," which was the legal equivalent of saying that a man falling from a building had a non-zero chance of learning to fly, which was technically true and practically the kind of thing you said when you wanted to give people permission to keep breathing for another few minutes.

The room received this opinion with the silence it deserved.

The intelligence officer, Lieutenant Ahn, proposed hacking the Auditors' data systems to backdate the petitions on Form 27-B. She had a plan. She had had, in fact, a contingency plan for this category of scenario since Year Three. The plan involved exploiting a vulnerability she believed existed in the Bureau's Q-band transmission protocols—a belief based on an anomaly in a signal return she had detected in Year Five and had been analyzing, in her off-hours, with the patient intensity of a woman embroidering a parachute during free fall. She presented the plan with crisp slides and a timeline. The timeline was six months. She did not mention, because she did not need to, that nobody knew what the "applicable appeals window" was, or whether six months fell inside it or had already passed, seventeen years ago, while they were busy filling out the wrong form.

The captain listened. The room listened. The intercom crackled with the breathing of three thousand people who had once been citizens of nations, members of families, holders of opinions about sports teams and breakfast cereals and whether it was acceptable to recline one's seat on an airplane, and who were now a single entry in a galactic filing system, a species-level line item drifting through the dark on the strength of a footnote and a form number that didn't exist.

From the back of the room, a woman raised her hand.

She was seated in the last row, which was technically not a row but a bench fashioned from a decommissioned ventilation panel that someone had bolted to the wall in Year Six to accommodate overflow seating. She sat at its far end, near the door, in the posture of someone accustomed to waiting—not the restless, performative waiting of people who believed their waiting would be noticed and rewarded, but the deep, geological waiting of a person who had internalized the understanding that systems move at the speed systems move at, and no amount of sighing would change this.

Her name was Gladys Okafor-Weinberg, and she had spent twenty-three years at the Ohio Bureau of Motor Vehicles, Branch 412, on Route 40 outside of Zanesville, the one between the defunct Arby's and the tire shop with the inflatable gorilla, the one with the overhead fluorescents that buzzed at a frequency later determined to be clinically associated
